chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibn Abi Ahmad, from one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: 'Does the person in Ihram hunt game, then ransom it, and then eat it or discard it?' He said: 'In that case, there would be another ransom upon him.' I said: 'So what should he do with it?' He said: 'He should bury it.'

If it were not for the fact that it follows the ruling of the carcass (dead animal), as contained in the earlier reports, he would not have ordered its burial, but rather ordered that he feed those who are in Ihram, and not impose another ransom.

The Shaykh (peace be upon him) said: 'And the person in Ihram does not eat the locusts, up to his saying: and the tree, if its base is in the Sanctuary.' That has all passed, so there is no reason to repeat it. Then he said (peace be upon him): 'And the tree, if its base is in the Sanctuary and its branch in the open, it is forbidden, and likewise if its base is in the open and its branch in the Sanctuary.'

key_terms.الْحِلُّ: The Open/normal state outside the Sanctuary
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: The person in Ihram (state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What should a person in Ihram do with hunted game to avoid additional ransom?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the principle of *fida* (ransom) by explaining that burying the hunted game prevents it from being treated as a *maytah* (carcass) requiring a second penalty, thereby distinguishing between consumption and mere disposal. The text further extends the sanctity of the Haram to botanical entities, ruling that trees are forbidden if either their root or their branches extend into the sacred boundary, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the prohibition.
